utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Call the case, please, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-98-34-T, the Prosecutor versus Naletilic and Martinovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the delay because we don't have much time to lose. Yes, Mr. Seric? Would you please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. My learned friends, when Emile Zola was asked, after he had written his well-known text, "J'accuse," in relation to the notorious Dreyfus Affair, why had he addressed a court case, why he, a writer, got involved in law? Why was he writing as if he were a lawyer? And Zola responded to those who criticised him or rather he wrote, "Gentlemen, why do you separate life from law or law from life?" Meaning the facts. "And that is why this terrible judicial mistake has occurred. One needs to address at the same time the Court and the public, inform the former and the later learn about life and about law because that is the only way how you can be protected as well." Yesterday, we adjourned when I was about to indicate how we shall be going to prove that Vinko Martinovic did not exercise direct or indirect control over the members of his unit, as is alleged by the Prosecution. The Defence claims that the act constituting a crime, an accused may perpetrate alone or together with others. The pursued criminal intent rests with the fact that the accused acted with the indispensable intent of committing a crime under international criminal law. The Defence claims that planning, as a form of -- is a form of vicarious criminal responsibility and that the elements of that particular crime are the same as in the crime of aiding and abetting. Moreover, planning is a form of complicity in which the criminal responsibility emerges only after the crime has been committed. The Defence therefore claims that there is no precedent to support the theory that planning of the crime, as laid down by the Statute, can per se be punishable as a separate stage in the commission of such crimes. A person may be punished either for the planning of a crime or for its commission, but not for both, because the perpetrator may not be punished for the planning as a separate stage in the commission of a crime. The Defence claims that instigation is a narrowly defined crime, when the act of instigation needs to be very concrete, both with regard to the perpetrator and the crime in order to prevent the violation of the legitimate freedom of speech. The pursued actus reus, the pursued crime consists in the fact that first the accused has committed an act with a direct intent of provoking a certain executor or a recognisable group that the executor belongs to, to commit a specific crime. Secondly, there is a causal relationship between the act defined as instigation and a concrete crime. The criterion is the causality standard, had it not been for because one cannot speak about instigation if the perpetrator has already decided to commit a crime. I think that it is very important. The Defence believes that there must exist a very strict condition of mens rea, of criminal intent for instigation. A person instigating must intend to directly encourage or provoke a concrete executor, a concrete perpetrator or a recognisable group that the latter belongs to commit a specific crime, whose commission the instigator aspires to. An instigator must not only be aware of all the elements of the crime, the commission of which he instigates but he must also be possessed of the same intent as the perpetrator. The Defence claims that the instigator is criminally liable only within the constraints of his personal intent, regardless of the responsibility of the chief perpetrator. The Defence also claims that they can be no ordering if there -- if the relationship between the superior and subordinate is lacking, because it does not suffice to simply be authorised to issue orders. A superior would, in addition to that, need to order a particular person, who is subordinate to him to commit a concrete crime. The issue of general orders or orders related to general issues does not suffice. Between an order and a concrete crime, there is and must exist a causal relationship, and the criterion -- and the criterion, again, is the causality standard, had it not been for. There must also be a very strict condition of mens rea, if one is to determine criminal responsibility for issuing orders. The superior needed to be aware of all the elements which constitute a crime whose commission he has ordered and he also needed to aspire to it, that his subordinate commits a crime. To consider the superior criminally responsible for ordering the commission of a crime, one must show that he pursued the same intent as his subordinate, who is responsible for the perpetration. The important thing is the criminal intent, the mens rea of the superior, rather than that of the subordinate who carried out the order. This was said in the judgement in the Blaskic case. When it comes to aiding and abetting and participating in a joint intent or plan, the Defence claims that the pursuit actus reus has been met in those cases when the accused has helped to commit a particular crime by another person, and his assistance has directly and significantly contributed to the commission of a concrete crime, meaning that that crime would not have happened in the same manner, as likely as not, had the accused not behaved in the way he did, although the conduct of the accused did not have to be a condition conditio siue qua non - for the commission of the crime. It nevertheless, that is his conduct, had to have a certain influence. We claim that the presence of an accused suffices to establish aiding and abetting only, that is only, when this presence has directly and significantly contributed to it a specific crime. In supporting its argument that we shall put forward, the Defence refers to the findings of the Appeals Chamber in the Aleksovski case, where the judgement in the Tadic case is also quoted. An Article 7, paragraph 3 of the Statute shows clearly that three elements need to be proven in order to charge an individual with the superior responsibility for crimes committed by a subordinate. The first is the existence of the superiority and the subordination relationship between the accused and the perpetrator of the crime. The second is the awareness or rather the knowledge of the superior that his subordinate has committed or is about to commit a crime. The Defence claim that the superior-subordinate relationship needs to be such that the subordinate is subordinated to the command of a superior in a concrete military chain of command or his functional equivalent or if the superior is a civilian, he must have the same kind of control over the superior as a military commander would have had. The Appeals Chamber in the Celebici case defined the superior as an individual who has power or powers, either in de facto or in de jure form to prevent the commission of a crime by a subordinate or to punish the perpetrators of a crime after it has been committed. The same Chamber then proceeded to conclude that power or powers to prevent or punish do not emerge only from the de jure powers accorded through official designation, appointment. The Appeals Chamber thus supported the conclusion of the Trial Chamber in the Celebici case that the de facto superiors may be liable to criminal Prosecution if it is established that they had true and effective powers to control the behaviour of their subordinates. On the basis of the superior position, one might deem as criminally responsible not only persons holding formal command positions but also persons who are proven to have held effective command positions in more informal structures and who had been vested with powers to prevent or punish the commission of crimes by persons who were under their true control. In the absence of formal appointment, it is of utmost importance for the establishment of criminal responsibility, the genuine exercise of power and, in particular, the manifestation of effective control. Effective control is, among other things, has, among other things, been accepted in the judicial practice of the international court as a standard for the establishment of the responsibility of the superior. This effective control also needs to be proven in our case. The Defence claims that that was not the case, especially in the relationship between him and his subordinates. The effective control therefore needs to be proven also in those cases where one has superiors de jure and de facto under whose direct command was the subordinate. The role of the commander as such is covered by Article 87. The concept of a superior is much broader and needs to be viewed in the light of a hierarchy which also covers the control concept. Article 87, one of the additional protocol further then expands the legal obligation of commanders to properly supervise all their superiors, not only the soldiers under their command. The high contracting parties to this protocol and parties to the conflict will be -- will request from military commanders in relation to members of the armed forces and parties under their command and other persons under their control to prevent, and where necessary, put an end to the breaches of Geneva Conventions and this protocol and notify thereof relevant authorities. Therefore, only the persons holding positions of command either de jure or de facto either military or civilian who indubitably form part of the chain of command, either directly or indirectly, with the genuine power to control or punish the acts of their subordinates may be subjected to criminal responsibility. The Appeals Chamber in the same case that I mentioned earlier, established that the level of the de facto power or powers to exercise control, which is the condition pursuant to a doctrine on the command responsibility equals the level based on de jure powers. The existence of a superior position, be it de jure or de facto, be it military or civilian needs to be based on the assessment of the true powers of the accused in a specific case and the same holds true of our case as well. The official position of the authorities may be established through the existence of an official appointment or formal powers with which somebody is vested. The positions in the army are usually very strictly defined and the existence much a clear chain of command based on a strict hierarchy makes it easier to prove generally speaking the chain of command will cover different levels of hierarchy, starting from the definition of the policies at the highest level down the chain of command to its translation into life on the ground. At the top of this chain, political front men may define political goals. The strategic command will then translate those goals into concrete military plans in cooperation with high government authorities. At the next level, this plan is forwarded to high military commanders responsible for operative zones. The last link in the chain of command is the level of tactical commanders who directly command the troops. Your Honours, my question is not merely rhetorical. It is a proper question to be asked in this case, and we shall clear it up in our case. Where is, in this chain of command, where is my client, Vinko Martinovic, in this chain? Nowhere. And we shall prove that. The element of consciousness, which is required pursuant to Article 7(3) of the Statute, is divided into two different types of situations. The first one, the first situation, requires the superior to be aware that his subordinates are either committing or about to commit a crime. In the second situation, there was a -- the superior had reason to know that the subordinate was about to commit such acts or had done so. As far as the indispensable element of the consciousness is concerned, the first situation, in which the superior knows, is in the know, does not seem contradictory, the real knowledge that can be defined as consciousness, as the awareness that the relevant crimes were either committed or are to be committed may be proven by direct evidence or circumstantial evidence. Circumstantial evidence allows for them to be a base for the following conclusion. The subordinate must have been aware of the crimes committed by his subordinates. Depending on the position of the authority and the level of authority of the superior, therefore, whether it was a military or a civilian position, either de jure or de facto, depending on his level of responsibility within the chain of command, the evidence which is required to prove the actual, the real, knowledge, the real awareness, may be different. For example, the actual awareness of a military commander is easier to prove if one takes into consideration the fact that he is probably a member of an organised structure who is bound by defined systems of reporting. In the case of a de facto commander of a less formal military structure or civilian officials who are de facto in the positions of power, the standard of proving the fact must be higher and the burden of proof is on the Prosecution and not on the Defence. The Defence claims that the allegations, "he had a reason to know," refers to a situation in which the superior has the material information which, if it was analysed, would indicate that the subordinates are about to commit a crime or had committed a crime. It is alleged that without the evidence on the criminal activities of the subordinate, the omission of the commander of the superior and his failure to carry out an investigation according to the Defence, does not imply the superior's responsibility. In the Celebici case, the Trial Chamber adopted a good legal approach, when it rejected the standard, "he had the reason to know." The Defence here claims that the standard for -- to prove the control can be found in Article 86(1) of the supplementary protocol 1, in the way that this Article was interpreted in the Celebici case. It was established that the command responsibility cannot be proven on the basis of the fact that the commander should have invested more effort in order to learn about the behaviour of his subordinates. When we talk about a failure to take the necessary and reasonable measures in order to prevent or punish the perpetrators, the Defence claims that the measures have to be indispensable and reasonable, that they have to be inconsistent with the situation, as perceived by the commander, and not from putting the situation in a broader perspective. Further on, one must prove that the subordinate had the legal authority in order to undertake certain measures, and furthermore, that he had a material, substantive possibility to do that. According to this defence, between a failure of the subordinate to take a measure and subsequent commission of a crime, there must be a cause. What is important here, what is the most important here, when it comes to establishing the relationship of -- between a subordinate and a superior, is the effective authority allowing the subordinate to take measures. The formal authority to take measures must be interpreted within this context in assessing whether the subordinate has indeed failed to undertake certain measures. This Trial Chamber, in this case, has to go beyond the formal authority if he had them at all. I'm implying my client. And see whether he had any material possibilities to undertake certain measures. We are going to prove that such authority, Vinko Martinovic, did not have. The punishment and the duty -- and the task and duty to punish somebody appears naturally after the crime has been committed. People who become in charge of the command after the crime was committed are under the same obligation. This implies a duty to carry out an investigation in order to establish facts and to report to the superiors about these crimes. Your Honours, I know that after this presentation of our part of the case, I am going to say something that may sound funny and that may belong to a closing brief rather than an opening statement, but when things are added and subtracted, to speak in arithmetic terms, the conclusion is that my client is here by mistake, that he is sitting on -- in this courtroom by mistake, and that he has ended in the prison here in Scheveningen by mistake. Your Honours, the acts of crime may be committed only with predetermination, with -- they cannot be committed by accident. And the Prosecutor is trying to prove that. If there is no premonition on the parts of Vinko Martinovic, I have to prove that, and I must tell you that in our presentation of evidence, we will try to prove that and I hope we will succeed. Your Honours, I must say that I'm not sitting in front of the knights of the round table and I do not expect that King Arthur will appear and decide by a simple gesture, by simple strike of a sword. I'm here sitting in front of you, Judges, but let me ask you: Can we separate facts from the law? Is it not the job of our lawyers -- of us lawyers? Do I have to speak about the law only in my closing brief? What the Defence is going to prove from the legal aspect, this may be too late, and it would be even later still in the appeals. You're not a jury, fortunately or luckily, but you are people, and I'm not speaking in abstract terms. Everybody here in the courtroom has to be a human being first and foremost. Sophocles rightfully says the following about the man in Antigone. He says, "there are very many great things but nothing is greater than the human being. The beasts, the animals, everything is less worthy than the man." Athens in the period of Sophocles had about 400.000 inhabitants, some of them rich, some of them poor, some of them peasants, some of them noblemen. It was full of different peoples, people who were not citizens of Athens. Some of them were foreigners some of they are were slaves, craftsmen, tradesmen and they belonged to all races and religions. Sophocles is not concerned with anybody's origin, with anybody's wealth, with anybody's religion. He speaks about the man, the human being, who can be good and bad, who can be wise or stupid, so the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. real man, as the man is. Ernest Bloch also wrote about human beings and said that "people are volatile beings and they resemble nature because the nature is also volatile. It can be magnificent. It can be kind and generous but it can also be cruel. And so can the human -- the man. Today, the man is reflection of the volatility of the nature which surrounds him." "Over the time, the man is fighting for survival. He is being -- he is suffering cold and heat. He is being destroyed by earthquakes and floods. He suffers from epidemics. But the man goes on. He has learned how to wage a war against the nature and animals. Unfortunately he has also learned how to destroy everything around him. The man has conquered and is -- continues to conquer the nature. He is discovering its laws. He is mastering the laws of nature. Both to his benefit as well as to his detriment." "The man's restlessness and curiosity have turned him into the conqueror of the earth, the sea and the sky. He is now travelling at the light -- at the speed of wind and sound. He concurs mountains and depths of the sea. Here, on the Earth, he defies nature, he changes it and creates life. He has created robots to work instead of him. The wisdom of the human being has discovered a lot of things but there are still a number of questions in the nature that surrounds him, in the space above him, and the question is where from, where to, what and why? And thus and hence the reason for his restlessness that will accompany him in the future." Now my colleague, Mr. Par, is going to continue with his part of the opening statement. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Par, to keep the consistence of the opening statement could I suggest that we make a break until you finish your presentation? Or you believe your statement is too long that we have to make a break during it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I plan to finish within one hour, so maybe you should decide whether we should break now or later on. I don't really mind one way or another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We will hear your statement, then we'll break.

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, in this part of the presentation, I intend to present the views of the Defence for Vinko Martinovic, according to the counts of the indictment and I wish to tell you how we want to proceed in the presentation of the Defence case. By the indictment, the Prosecutor of the International Criminal Tribunal has charged Vinko Martinovic with several crimes, crimes against humanity, grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions, the violation of laws and customs of war allegedly committed in Mostar from the period from April 1993 until the end of January 1994. That is during the armed conflict between Croats and Bosniaks in the area of Mostar. By their content, these crimes comprise persecutions of Bosnian Muslims, forced labour and inhumane treatment of prisoners of war, torture, murder, alternatively qualified as cruel treatment and causing pain, forceful resettlement of Bosnian Muslims and destruction and looting of their property. During the presentation of his case, the Prosecutor tried to prove that Vinko Martinovic is responsible on -- for all of these charges, either as an individual or according to the principle of command responsibility. In order to prove his case, the Prosecutor used documents obtained from military archives, from the AID, the secret Muslim police, as the Prosecutor himself calls it, various international intelligence sources. We heard testimonies by different international experts and witnesses, Bosnian Muslims, victims of war, who had all previously been

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: mercenaries, who had joined the war for motives which were certainly not honourable. The objective of all this evidence was to substantiate the indictment and turn Vinko Martinovic, a common foot soldier and commander of a small unit on the separation line, into the main culprit for all the evil that happened in Mostar. Many persons, many services, and secret services were interested to see Vinko Martinovic sacrificed, and that the real perpetrators and those who gave orders could hide behind his back, but the Prosecutor's case already showed that the way Vinko Martinovic is portrayed in the indictment is simply unsustainable. In the presentation of its case, Vinko Martinovic's Defence will present to this Honourable Court evidence by which it will address every count in the indictment and prove that Vinko Martinovic is not responsible for the crimes he has been charged with. We shall prove that Vinko Martinovic has been offered to this Tribunal as a scapegoat by Bosnian and Croat secret services, who acted in concert with representatives of the international community and who, after a well organised media campaign, chose Vinko Martinovic as the person who was the easiest to be brought before this Tribunal, because he does not have any political backing, because he's not a member of any political party or option, because nobody protects him, he has no political influence, he has no political friends who could complicate his extradition, and here he is now before this Tribunal, answerable for the things that he has nothing whatsoever to do with, to answer for the plans of the Republic of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna to answer for the establishment of the Heliodrom, to answer for the resettlement of the civilian population, to answer for the participation in an international conflict, to answer for the things that he saw for the first time when he saw the indictment. The accused before this Tribunal know only too well that they have to fear most the parts of the indictment that they don't understand. The parts of the indictment where they are not even mentioned, the factual context, the general assumptions of the indictment. In other words, the general prejudices which have been created by them, about them, and about the war, in which they participated, by the CNN and other international or local media who simplified the war and split the participants in the war into good guys and bad guys. The task of this Defence is to return Vinko Martinovic to the separation line in Mostar, to the Bulevar street in front of the health centre, medical centre, where he was with his group of some 40 soldiers, from the first day to the last day of the conflict. It is our task to bring him out, to take him out of the big picture, portraying an international conflict, to bring him and take him out of the political plans devised -- designed in Zagreb and Mostar, because it is simply not his place to be there, and the Prosecution -- Prosecutor himself did not show any proof that would tie him to any of these plans. Vinko Martinovic did not have any political or military authorities, and therefore he could neither participate or create systemic campaigns that might have negative impacts relative to the political goals that can be reduced to the division of Bosnia and Herzegovina. The main thesis of the Defence, with regard to all of these allegations in the indictment, is that Vinko Martinovic participated in the conflict between Bosniaks and Croats in Mostar in 1993, but he did not participate in the implementation of the plans to divide Bosnia and Herzegovina, as has been implicated by the indictment. Although we are aware of the fact that negative facts do not have to be proven, still, the Defence is going to use witnesses and documents in order to prove that thesis during the presentation of their case. The second thesis of the Defence that we are going to prove is that Vinko Martinovic, at the beginning of the war in Mostar, was in the same position as all the other able-bodied individuals, i.e. that he did not have a possibility or a reason to avoid participation in this conflict. The war in Mostar started with a Serbian aggression. Vinko Martinovic joined the defence of his town, together with his neighbours, Muslims and Croats. He became a HOS commander, known for his courage and decisiveness. On 9 May, 1993, the conflict between Croats and Muslims started in Mostar for reasons unbeknown to Vinko Martinovic, and again he did not have either a choice or a reason not to join the defence of his neighbourhood, his house. He finds a position on the separation line, and this self-organised defence later on resulted in the establishment of his unit. He became the commander of that unit. He is placed under the command of the town. And this is where he stayed until the end of the war. There were thousands of such soldiers in Mostar like Vinko Martinovic, on both sides of the town , people who found themselves in the while wind of the war against their will and in that war they joined military units in the way dictated to them by the circumstances. In both parts of the cities, of the town, there were such commanders as Vinko Martinovic. There were dozens of them. His command responsibility was based on his special authority towards a group of soldiers that he commanded in the conditions of a self-organised army, without the existence of a firm military structure and without any real command over the unit which was composed of volunteers, who were kept in the army only by their personal motive to defend their own homes. What did that unit do on the separation line? Did they commit war crimes? Did Vinko Martinovic, as their commander, was responsible for that as the Prosecution claims that he was? The Defence is going to prove that Vinko Martinovic in his capacity as the commander of the ATG Mrmak unit which was later on renamed and became the Vinko Skrobo ATG is not responsible for the crimes that -- with which he is charged by the indictment. Count 1 of the indictment is entitled, "Persecutions." In this count, Vinko Martinovic is charged with the persecution based on political, racial and religious basis, which is qualified as crime against humanity, which is punishable by Articles 5(H), 7(1) and 7(3) of the Statute of the International Criminal Tribunal. The crimes which are relevant to Vinko Martinovic in this count are given in paragraphs 26 to 30 and 32 and 34 and represent the central point of this indictment, because by their general incrimination, they compose, they comprise all the other acts which are mentioned in the indictment. Paragraph 1, count 1, of the indictment says that in the critical period, that is between April 1993 and January 1994, Vinko Martinovic, as the commander of the Mrmak unit, together with other leaders, agents and members of the HV and HVO, planned, aided, ordered committed or instigated the systematic persecution of civilians, Bosnian Muslims, on political, racial, national or religious basis in the entire area for which it was claimed that it belonged to the HZ HB or HR HB, and that he did that by the following means: by unlawfully detaining, forcibly transferring and deporting civilians, Bosnian Muslims, that he exposed Bosnian Muslims to torture, inhumane acts, murders and wilful deprivation of life, causing sufferings, using Bosnian Muslims for forced labour and as human shields, destruction and looting of buildings and plundering of public and private property, and so on and so forth. Therefore, these incriminations, persecution, comprise all the other acts which are mentioned in other counts of the indictment, effectively all the other crimes are consumed by the count 1 of the indictment. Therefore, we believe that it is absolutely unsustainable to qualify them separately and ask for the accused to be -- to be held responsible for one crime under different qualifications. Just briefly, by such legal qualifications, the accused is brought into a more difficult position than the one he would have if he was tried in the country where the crimes were allegedly committed, the country whose citizen he is and whose citizens are both the accused and the aggrieved persons. This is the basic objection to -- of the Defence to the legal qualifications in the indictment, and represents the request for the equality of arms which is the basic right of the accused. However, let's go back to count 1. In contrast with this Prosecution's allegation, the Defence claims that the Prosecution's charges are incorrect and it will prove that the accused Vinko Martinovic did not commit crimes under this count. The Defence will show that during the period covered by the indictment, Vinko Martinovic had no military or political powers that could link him with the planning, instigation or commission or any strategic acts in Mostar, let alone the area of Herzegovina as such, and that he was no well-known ill-famed executor of ethnic cleansing against the Bosnian Muslim population as the Prosecutor alleges. This picture lacks foundation and it is what the indictment is based on, supported by Bosnian and Croatian media and, again, supported, propped up, by doubtful and fabricated information of the Bosnian and Croatian secret services, all with a view to meeting the interests of the international community to find persons to be tried for crimes committed during the war, at all costs, so that the war could finally be put an end to it and so that other international projects in Bosnia-Herzegovina could start to be translated into life. However, this time, the person of the accused was picked out by wrongly because he objectively, in view of the position that he held, could not commit all the crimes that he is charged with, and therefore, he can not either assume the responsibility, the burden of responsibility for others who were above him or next to him, that is the plan to shift the burden to Vinko Martinovic cannot succeed if the trial is fair. Witnesses for the Defence and some documents which were disclosed to the Defence by the Prosecution will attest to that. Small, ordinary people who are personally persecuted, the detainees of the Heliodrom, the detainees in the Vinko Skrobo unit will testify about that. They will speak about the role of Vinko Martinovic in the war in Mostar, about the establishment and tasks of his unit, his treatment and attitude to Muslims during that critical period of time, how Vinko Martinovic protected Muslims against persecution, how Muslims came to him to seek protection, how they asked when detained to be allotted to his unit because they would feel safe there. They will speak about the conflict, which existed in Mostar at the time, and they will speak about the chaos which reigned in Mostar at the time when the conflict between Croats and Muslims started they will talk about military gangs, dressed in HVO military uniforms, who evicted Muslims from their flats and plundered their property by misrepresenting themselves and saying that they were members of Stela's units, using false names like calling themselves Stela or "Stela's boys," and also referring to false orders allegedly issued by Stela and the like. The Prosecution's documents testify to that. These witnesses will testify about Stela's reactions in those cases when he would be told that persecution was being carried out in his name. The Defence will show that the unit under Vinko Martinovic's command had a task which required its permanent presence at the demarcation line and that around the town, there were different units arrived from other parts of Herzegovina who committed crimes together with certain groups in Mostar. Vinko Martinovic's unit, with the limited number of people which was somewhere between 50 and 80, throughout the war held one of the most vulnerable points at the demarcation line and never left that front line and they did not do that because otherwise, it would have opened a passage for the enemy to break through into the west part of the town. Therefore, it was objectively not possible for this unit to abandon the front line and join the tasks of the systematic persecution in Mostar and in Herzegovina, as is alleged by the Prosecution. The witnesses for the Defence will explain to the Court the role of this unit in two major waves of persecution, as the Prosecution alleges which according to paragraph 26 of the indictment happened on the 9th of May, 1993, and early July, 1993. These witnesses will explain that the unit under Vinko Martinovic's command, originally called Mrmak and subsequently Vinko Skrobo, did not even exist on the 9th of May, 1993, although Vinko Martinovic, and many members of this future unit participated in the fighting on the 9th of May, 1993, but they did so having self-organised themselves to defend their homes and their neighbourhoods. The Defence will prove its postulate that Vinko Martinovic cannot even theoretically be held accountable for persecutions performed on the 9th of May, 1993, because at that time he was not -- he did not command any unit and did not participate in any persecution. A unit under his command was formed only later, that is towards the end of that May 1993, when the military situation in the city became more stable and when the military organisation at the town level was set up. In relation to alleged persecutions happened in July 1993, we shall show that this unit did not participate in it because at that time it was manning the participation line next to the health centre on the Bulevar in Mostar. So the question hanging in the air is who then persecuted Muslims in West Mostar, who is it that turned, that made Vinko Martinovic into an accused for these persecutions? And how did this happen? If this thing is not true and the other thing is not true, then how did all this come to pass? The Prosecutor's thesis of the planned, systematic implementation of ethnic cleansing with the planners in Zagreb, with the operatives in Herzegovina and the executors in the streets of Mostar is to our mind a bureaucratic, a paper thesis which runs counter to the nature of the so-called ethnic cleansing. We deem that ethnic cleansing, once it starts, becomes an unstoppable process which follows its own momentum and that there is no need for a plan or a planner, because ethnic cleansing Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. already includes, already subsumes a drive, an inertia to move on. Because it is very simple: "I expel you. You expel my brother. You plunder me, I plunder your brother. You set my church on fire, so I put fire to your mosque." And that is the governing principle. Now, who is then the one who does it? Who plans that? Well, it is being done by people who have been expelled. Those who have been expelled, who have become expellees. Those who have already been ethnically cleansed from their homes or villages. However, that individual is nowhere in the uniform of his army. He goes, looks for a place under the sun. He looks for a new home. And how will he find one? He'll expel somebody else. Ergo, persecution is performed by former -- by the expelled persons. The plunder is done by the plundered, expulsions by the expelled. So it is a process which once -- which starts with the first plundered house, with the first destroyed house of worship, with the first expelled person, and how does it stop? Well, it stops when everybody has lost the security of one's home, where everything has been plundered and finally when the international community arrives to take stock of things. Ergo, it is not indisputable, it is said in this courtroom, that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, this method, called ethnic cleansing, was introduced by Serbs. At the time of the Serbian aggression on Bosnia-Herzegovina, and that process could not bypass the streets of the town of Mostar. Nobody had to plan how to do it in Mostar, because that particular wind finds its own corridors and it blows away everything that it meets in its way. The Defence will set out to prove, through its witnesses, that the citizens of Mostar, of all ethnicities, who happened in Mostar at the time of the Croat-Bosniak conflict, that Vinko Martinovic and his comrades in arms, people from his part of the town, simply happened to be in their heart of -- at the heart, at the centre of the fighting in Mostar, the fighting that he did not want, did not plan, did not instigate, but he sided with that side which brought together members of his people and the neighbours from his street, he fought at one particular point with the only single idea in his mind to defend his home. At the same time, things happened in this town which were absolutely beyond his grasp, that he had no say in, in which he had no hand, and for which he may not be held accountable. And now we come back to this question, who then expelled those Muslims from West Mostar and who is it that turned Vinko Martinovic into an accused for persecutions? How did that come to pass? And we can ask some further questions but who expelled Serbs from Mostar? Where are the Serbs? Who expelled Croats from East Mostar? Who is accused for the expulsion of Serbs and Croats from Mostar? How did that happen? Did -- was that ethnic cleansing too? Perhaps there is some other expression which does not associate a criminal responsibility. Serbs, Croats and Muslims expelled one another from Mostar. They were expelling one another, because such a war befell them that did not -- that did not allow you to feel safe in the enemy territory. There is no state, there is no police, there is no regular troops, there is only war, which has escaped control. Some left of their own. Others fled. The third were expelled. The fourth were captured. And their houses were moved into by those who had been expelled from their own houses. And that is how the town was partitioned. The war put on the citizens of Mostar in Bosnia-Herzegovina the uniforms of their peoples and pursuing their own survival, they expelled one another from their homes. Witnesses for the Defence, ordinary, small people know this story because that story is their lot, and they know only too well that there is no individual who could be marked in a manner in which Vinko Martinovic, Stela, is marked by this indictment. There is no such individual. Witnesses for the Defence will tell us how tales were spun and yarns told about heroes of war or criminals in order to encourage one and intimidate others with a view to propaganda, political -- pursuit of political and military goals in order to dissimulate one's fear and for hundreds of other reasons and that is how the story grew about Stela as a hero in the liberation of the city, to then the story about him as a war criminal who needs to be surrendered to The Hague Tribunal. Witnesses, active participants, in the media coverage of the war in Mostar and witnesses acquainted with the work of secret services at the time will testify how certain centres of political power used the media to prepare or organise actions, the purpose of which was to present Vinko Martinovic in a manner in which he is treated by the -- in the indictment today, so that he could be transferred to The Hague Tribunal. His transfer to the Tribunal met the request of the international community, and that was a simple one: Give me somebody to account for crimes in Mostar, give somebody -- give me somebody like Vinko Martinovic. Why he? Because he holds no political position, he holds no military post. He has no political friends, he has no political patron, he has absolutely -- he can not reveal any major secrets, and whether he comes here, then all of a sudden he'll be disclosing all sorts of secrets. No, he can not do that why not? Because he was never present in the decision making places in any case, he is nevertheless sufficiently well known to it appear as somebody very important, to see as a person who could be held accountable for it. In close relationship with count 1, persecutions, are also charges in the indictment related to forcible transfer of the population, plunder of private and public property, described in paragraphs 18 and 21, and qualified as grave breaches of the Geneva Conventions of 1949 and violations of the laws or customs of war. Although the Defence deems that during its case, the Prosecutor has not produced a single -- any relevant evidence regarding facts indicated in this -- in these counts, the Defence will prove that Vinko Martinovic and his unit never and in no way participated in the commission of these crimes. With regard to the forcible transfer of the population, the Defence claims that Vinko Martinovic's unit did not abandon the separation line and thus could not participate in possible actions involving the expulsion of the population. It is another Defence's thesis that no forcible transfer of the population took place, in the sense in which it is claimed by the Prosecution. They were organised transfers of the moves of the population from one to the other part of the town, across the separation line, but these moves from one to another part of the town were not forcible. Those were moves, transfers, organised by some humanitarian and other organisations and in agreement between -- in agreement reached between military and political structures in the two parts of the town at the request of citizens who themselves wanted to leave a certain part of the town for personal reasons, safety reasons, reunification of families and the like. In decision-making, concerning these moves of the population and organisation of the transfers, Vinko Martinovic and his unit played no role, except being a unit on the line who were therefore bound to enable an unobstructed and safe crossing of the civilians across the front line at the orders of the superior command. Witnesses for the Defence, soldiers from his unit, citizens from Mostar and the detainees in the unit will confirm these claims. With regard to the charges under item 1 -- 21, excuse me, on the plunder of public and private property, it is the Defence's postulate that the Prosecutor has not produced relevant evidence with regard -- that would concern Vinko Martinovic, but the Defence will, through its witnesses, soldiers from the unit, detainees in the unit and citizens who were exposed to the plunder of their property, to prove that Vinko Martinovic and his unit did not commit these crimes. We shall prove that there were numerous cases in which diverse criminal gangs which plundered misrepresented themselves as members of the Stela's unit or Stelici, Stela's boys, and we shall also prove that Vinko Martinovic has always reacted very harshly in order to very strictly in order to prevent such situations and plunders and even personally, he addressed the citizens of Mostar by radio requesting that all the cases of plunder and persecution in which somebody referred to his unit or brought up the name of his unit be reported. Vinko Martinovic personally took under custody all of the soldiers that he would catch in the act of plunder and always went to the rescue of citizens who had reported attempts to plunder their property. Counts 2 to 8, unlawful labour and live shields as inhuman treatment and wilful killing. Within the context of the indictment, within these counts, the indictment starts from the existence of the Heliodrom Camp from which prisoners of war were sent to work in individual units and on such occasions they were exposed to inhuman treatment. During its case, the Defence will produce witnesses who will be detainees from the Heliodrom, who were sent to work in the unit commanded by Vinko Martinovic. We shall also have as our witnesses soldiers from this unit and witnesses who were familiar with the situation regarding the detainees in this unit. We shall also produce certain documents disclosed to us by the Prosecution which show how the detainees from the Heliodrom were sent to individual units. These -- this evidence will show that the accused Vinko Martinovic had nothing to do with either the formation or the management of the centre at the Heliodrom or other detention centres, that neither he nor his units were part of any organised unit in detention centres. They will also show that not a single detainee in the Heliodrom was arrested by Vinko Martinovic's unit and that this unit has never had its own prisoners of war. The evidence will show that under the orders of the command of the Mostar defence and -- was how the detainees were sent to work in individual units rather than pursuant to orders from individual units. Individual units could not independently take prisoners from the Heliodrom because the detainees were under the jurisdiction of units which ran the Heliodrom and the commander of the defence of Mostar. Therefore all the responsibility for the treatment of prisoners of war rests exclusively with the administration of the Heliodrom and the command of the defence of Mostar and individual units such as the Vinko Skrobo ATG only performed -- only executed the orders of superior commands relative to prisoners of war. In a situation when all the able-bodied population were mobilised for Defence, the units were issued orders to take over prisoners of war so as to help them to perform individual jobs, and these units could not refuse to obey these orders and refuse to take up these detainees because that would mean to sabotage the defence tasks. The Defence will show that Vinko Martinovic in no manner whatsoever had a hand in the incarceration of civilians and prisoners of war in detention centres, that he absolutely had no hand in the detention centres, and that he never took any decisions concerning the use of prisoners of war in forced labour. Within this particular count of the indictment, it is alleged that these prisoners performed certain jobs on the fronts line under conditions -- under dangerous conditions because they were exposed to fire and that the mistreatment of prisoners took place. The Heliodrom detainees were being sent to work in this unit will testify in the Defence's case and they will tell us what was their position in the unit, they will tell it us about the conditions, about their living conditions, jobs that they had to perform, and whether they were indeed exposed to danger. And we shall then hear that in that particular unit, the detainees felt safer than in other units, and safer than at the Heliodrom itself. We shall also hear that some of them asked Stela to invite them to work in his unit so that they would not be assigned to some other units. We shall also hear that they partook of the same meals as the unit's soldiers in the restaurant called Hladovina, that they moved without any guards or supervision, that they went home to see the members of their families to have a bath, a change of clothes, that they were paid for individual jobs and the like. We shall also hear that none of the detainees was killed on the front line, which was in Stela's zone of responsibility and in the physical jobs which the detainees performed from time to it time in the unit's zone were under conditions which in no way endangered their lives. Namely it is quite true that on the confrontation line, the positions of the parties to the conflict were separated but only a few dozen metres. There was only a street between them, that is the Bulevar, and that from both sides of this front line one could see what was going on on the other side. On both sides, they were prisoners of war performing for those units individual physical jobs, and those prisoners could be told apart from the soldiers because they did not wear uniforms. Both parties knew that the non-uniformed people moving or working for the unit are prisoners of war and therefore they were in no danger of enemy fire because nobody wanted to fire at one's own people, and that was an unwritten rule. And the prisoners of war knew that and they were not at -- their life's were not at risk at that time when they were with the unit. Moreover, the unit also provided protection from the enemy fire, such as, for instance, a high walls made of high barriers made of sand bags or trenches that were dug, or cross trenches that offered safe protection to both soldiers and prisoners of war. From the detainees we shall hear that Vinko Martinovic Stela did not permit that the detainees be exposed to danger and also prohibited any harassment of the detainees or the inhumane treatment. We will hear from the detainees that they turned to Vinko Martinovic on several occasions asking for his help. They even asked him to intervene on their behalf so that they could be joined with their families and leave Mostar. In these cases, Vinko Martinovic helped them to obtain the necessary documents and so on and so forth. In these counts, a special place is given to the charges relative to 17 September, 1993, when Vinko Martinovic allegedly issued an order to give wooden rifles to the detainees who were supposed to go along a tank, and charges on using the detainees as a human shield, in which allegedly three of the detainees were killed. After the end of the presentation of his case, the Prosecutor abandoned the charges for the human shield and the Court made a decision that the Prosecution failed to prove the situation with the human shield and the killing of the detainees in the zone of Stela's unit. A similar story is with the rifle -- wooden rifles. We shall hear the testimonies of former members and detainees, from the unit, and they will talk about the events that took place on the 17th of September, 1993. This was a regular military operation in which all the units on the line took place. It was a failed and very short-lived operation which represented an attempt to move the separation line. We shall also hear testimonies of eye witnesses, participants in that operation, they will testify about the movement of the tank, they will say that there were no detainees with wooden rifles next to the tank. They will testify to the effect that the operation described in the indictment would have been illogical and undoable under the given circumstances. They will also testify to the fact that the story about the detainees, about wooden rifles, spread all over Mostar, that it was carried by newspapers and that that story was told by some detainees who fled across the separation line, that that story at the beginning was not linked with this particular unit, and that only later on, when the indictment against Stela became public, the story had it that the alleged soldier belonged to Stela's unit. Although the eye witnesses on -- and the participants in the event on the 17th of September, 1993, are all clear that this did not happen in the area of responsibility of the Vinko Skrobo unit. During this trial, we heard information that there is a wooden rifle, which according to the testimony of one Prosecution witness was taken away from him and stored in a museum. It was already proven during the Prosecution case that it was a false piece of evidence and this will be additionally proven by the Defence witnesses. Closely related to these counts is the interpretation found in counts 9 to 12 relative to the torture and wilful causing of suffering. Witnesses for the Defence, former members of the unit and detainees from the unit, will testify to the fact that Vinko Martinovic, Stela, never personally used force or tortured the detainees, that he prohibited his subordinates from doing so, and that in cases when he learned about any such instances, he took appropriate measures. We will also hear that Vinko Martinovic expelled from his unit a certain number of soldiers who were prone to alcohol, drugs and violence, and all for the reasons that these individuals were prone to maltreating detainees and that they were prone to criminal acts. Counts 13 to 17 talk about the murder, wilful killing and wilfully causing great suffering on Nenad Harmandic. Alternatively this crime has been qualified as cruel treatment, and this is the only charge of murder in this indictment. But even the Prosecutor was not sure that it was actually murder. That's why he alternatively qualified it as a cruel treatment. The Prosecution's allegation that Nenad Harmandic was brought to Vinko Martinovic's unit and that he was beaten and killed in that unit and that Vinko Martinovic knew about that, that he didn't do anything to prevent that and to punish the perpetrators, is not sustainable, and the Prosecutor's case has already shown that he does not have any proof for such an allegation. Contrary to that, the Defence claims the following: It is correct that Nenad Harmandic was brought together with a group of detainees from Heliodrom to the Vinko Skrobo unit but his condition was already very bad, he had been beaten already in the Heliodrom camp, where he had been regularly beaten by soldiers in Heliodrom and some other detainees who wanted to revenge themselves for Nenad Harmandic's doings during the time when he was an active policeman. The Defence will prove that Vinko Martinovic was not present whether Nenad Harmandic was brought to the unit and when he subsequently learned about his presence, he interviewed Nenad Harmandic, he saw his condition and on the same day he returned him to the Heliodrom. Former members of the unit will testify about the stay of Nenad Harmandic's in the Vinko Skrobo unit. Those members of the unit who were present during Harmandic's stay in the unit and they are the witnesses who are going to testify to the condition -- Harmandic's condition when he arrived in the unit and when he left the unit. During the presentation of the Defence case, we are going to hear two experts, doctors, and one forensic expert who are going to give their expert opinion on the evidence presented by the Prosecutor during the presentation of his case. The first of these pieces of evidence is the findings of Dr. Dobraca, Dr. Zuja; who performed the autopsy of the bodies excavated in Liska Park in Mostar and during the -- their post-mortem they identified one of the bodies as the body of Nenad Harmandic. During the Prosecutor's case the Defence disputed this identification and during the presentation of the Defence case, the forensic expert will point to the mistakes made during the post-mortem and the identification of the body carried out by Dr. Dobraca and Dr. Zuja. The Defence will also prove that the identification is a scientifically unreliable. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Another proof that the Prosecution presented and that the Defence intends to dispute, via one of his witnesses, expert witnesses, is the testimony by Witness HA. The Defence will present medical documents, medical documentation about the condition of health of that witness, and the expert psychiatrist will give the evaluation of the psychological condition of this witness based on this documentation. This expert testimony will show that this person is of such an impaired psychological condition that he cannot give credible testimony because he suffers from a grave impairment of memory, understanding and cognition. We will also hear witnesses who will talk about the testimonies of some of the Prosecutor's witnesses who presented their hearsay evidence as their own evidence, and the Defence will call these people who have personal knowledge about this information. So in short, this would be the main positions of the Defence, regarding the counts of the indictment that the Defence is going to dispute during the presentation of its case. We have envisaged the testimonies of a total of 35 witnesses, out of whom two will be expert witnesses. One of them background witness who will be talking about the military and political circumstances and the international conflict, will present a limited number of documents most of them furnished by the Prosecution during the presentation of the Prosecutor's case and the number of documents who will serve as the basis for expert witnesses' testimonies. Defence witnesses will testify in groups and according to themes, so we will have three basic groups of witnesses. One of them will be members, former members, of the unit who will testify about the circumstances relative to the units and the events that took place in the section -- on the section of the front line manned by the -- Vinko Martinovic's unit. They will also be talking about the circumstances of the attitude towards the detainees, persecution and the role of Vinko Martinovic and others. The second group of witnesses will consist of the former detainees from the Heliodrom who were assigned to work in the Vinko Skrobo unit and who spent a certain time in that unit as prisoners of war. These witnesses will talk about their personal experiences, relative to the attitude towards detainees, their position, and the attitude of Vinko Martinovic towards the detainees. The third group of witnesses will be comprised of the citizens of Mostar who lived in the western part of Mostar, close, in the vicinity of the Vinko Skrobo unit. They will present their personal information and knowledge about the persecution, looting of property and the role of Vinko Martinovic and his unit in this event. We will start with the last group first, and the soldiers will come last, because of some technical circumstances which dictated the schedule of our witnesses. In addition to these three groups of witnesses, we will have some other background witnesses who will talk about the general situation in Mostar and the role and position and the significance of Vinko Martinovic in the events which took place in Mostar. They will be talking about the targeted media and intelligence campaign aimed at sacrificing Vinko Martinovic as the person who could be charged with the crimes committed in Mostar. Vinko Martinovic's Defence has opted for a simple defence based on the testimonies of common people from Mostar who have suffered during the conflicts between Croats and Bosniaks. These people of various -- different ethnic backgrounds are direct eyewitnesses of all the events, and they will be asked to present, to share with us their personal experiences, to tell us what they saw and what they heard because we believe that this is the true story in which everybody knows who everybody was and what everybody did. These testimonies and other pieces of evidence which will be presented by the Defence during the Defence case will show that the indictment against Vinko Martinovic is not -- cannot be substantiated. The Defence will prove that Vinko Martinovic was just a foot soldier on the Defence line in an unnecessary conflict that he himself did not choose and that in his capacity, he participated in military operations but he did not commit any crimes that are -- that he is charged with, and -- either as an individual, either according to the principle of command responsibility. This would be all from me, Your Honours, and this brings my presentation to it the end. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You are exactly on time. We will have a break and after that, we will have our first witness in this case. We will resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Could we have our witness now? Yes, Mr. Usher, please bring in the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Witness. Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Will you please make the solemn declaration in accordance with the paper the usher is showing you, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may sit down, please. Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, can you please introduce yourself to the Honourable Court?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: My name is Jadranko Martinovic. I am Vinko Martinovic's brother.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, I'm going to give you some instructions in order to facilitate this testimony of yours. I have to emphasise one thing. The speed is not important. I'm referring to the speed of my questions and speed of your answers. The most important thing is for you to make a pause after my question and before you start giving your answer. Can you please use the screen that you have in front of you and try to follow the rate of the interpretation? You will see the black dot at the end of the sentence. When it stops, then you start giving your answer. It is going to make the life of our interpreters easier and believe me, although it may sound surprising, it will be even faster if you follow the simple instruction. What were your relationships with your brother Vinko Martinovic? Did you grow up and live together? Did you, during the war, maintain regular contact?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: We have brotherly relationship. We lived together in our family house, in one house, and we had normal relationship. There is nothing to say about that relationship. Throughout the war, we maintained regular contacts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the allegations in the indictment against Vinko Martinovic?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge about the events which are described in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of some of them, but not about all of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell the Honourable Court where does the knowledge come from, the knowledge about the events that you know of?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: During the war, I was in Mostar throughout the war, and I spent a lot of time with my brother, and in a certain way, I was a participant in the events that took place in the town of Mostar, and that is the origin of my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: At the beginning, can you tell us something about Vinko's life before the war? What did he do and what did he live on?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Vinko Martinovic had a lower educational degree. He finished school for apprentices. Mostar had a very well developed industrial production so it was very desirable in the town to have a trade, a craftsmanship, in order to be able to find employment in the town of Mostar. He worked for a very short time in his trade but he mostly engaged in commerce, and for a while he was also a taxi driver.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: From the time you spent with him, from the knowledge of his world views, could you tell us something about his positions, about Muslims and Serbs who lived in Mostar together with Croats? As we all know, as this Honourable Court knows.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I believe that he did not have any particular position. He mingled with them and I don't believe that anybody in Mostar had a position towards Muslims and Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you saying that nobody in Mostar actually cared what the other person's religion or ethnic background was? Is that what you were saying?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if anybody else cared or not, but our father, Vinko's and my father, finished his education in the school which was known as Mejtef. That was a Muslim school.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: After the changes in sociopolitical organisation and the breakdown of Yugoslavia was Vinko politically engaged in any organisation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did he, at the time, publicly show his political views and particularly views involving the relationship between Muslims, Croats and Serbs in Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the town of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you personally find political engagement at the time, or did you promote publicly some political or other options?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was your personal attitude towards the position of Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina, as it was at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think I had any particular position. Their position was the same as the position of all the other peoples.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you remember, during the Serb aggression against Mostar, where was your brother and how did he react to the Serbian aggression against Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: During the Serbian aggression against Mostar, my brother resided in the -- in one of the Mostar neighbourhoods whose name is Rodoc. This neighbourhood is in the vicinity of the former airport, the former military airport, which was the first to be occupied by the Serbian Army or the Yugoslav People's Army, whatever it was at the time. And therefore, this was the first unsecure -- insecure area of residence in Mostar and this is where the first houses were destroyed and set on fire. In the vicinity of that place. Several thousands of people abandoned that neighbourhood when the first skirmishes started and Vinko was among those people. Most of those people spread all over the town and Vinko found himself in a village in the vicinity of Mostar, where he joined a HOS unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What happened at the time with you personally?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was in the town, like everybody else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What was this HOS? What kind of an organisation was it, the one that Vinko Martinovic joined?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, in Mostar, HOS was the first military formation, if you can call it a military formation, with some kind of weapons, and ready to engage in actions against the Serbian army, who were trying to block the roads, that is to obstruct our movement, so they were the only ones which gave us some feeling of security because it was the only organisation which offered some resistance when everything else looked pretty hopeless.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know who were Vinko's comrades at arms in that HOS unit at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, when the Serbian troops, that is the Yugoslav People's Army came to Mostar, after the airport, that is the military airport, which they took, they also took a considerable part of the east side of Mostar. Those people, those boys who had already been in a way expelled from their homes, that is some because of fear, some because they found it physically impossible to live anywhere else, joined HOS, so they were say in the beginning, in the early days, a considerable number of Serbs and Croats too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you aware then, or do you know today, what were the HOS objectives in Mostar at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: They had only one objective, to liberate the town, or rather to drive away those Yugoslav military units from the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you're asking me about my brother. Of course I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you discuss it with Vinko at the time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, of course, I don't know how this will sound but I'd like to say that my mother, my brother, my sister, my wife, my children and Vinko's family also, and many other families, Muslim and Croat, left the town of Mostar. Mostar became a dead town. Shells were falling. There was nobody to look after our laundry. We didn't have enough to eat. So in organisation I was the one who was responsible for that kind of things, to see to the laundry and things, and that is why we were together quite often at that time in those days.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And where did you become active in HOS at that time too? Or in some other formation?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The instruction, well, no, not instruction, but it was acceptable for everybody to report in his neighbourhood community or the municipality, to get some assignment. Somebody would be sent to clear the ruins, somebody else. And that is how I reported to the neighbourhood community, the one that I lived in, and I was assigned to the 4th Battalion of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did Vinko Martinovic have a commanding role in HOS?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Martinovic was the commander of the HOS staff in Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And Vinko's role in HOS, and in the struggle against the Serbian aggressor, how was it viewed by the citizens of Mostar? I mean all Mostarians regardless of their ethnic origin?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, it was the first war for all of us, and I do not -- I cannot wish to anyone to experience it. You have a rifle in your hands and do not know what to do with it. And I think this applies to eight out of ten men, when somebody -- someone has enough courage to bring together a dozen or so people then gradually the number begins to increase and then you hear some gunfire in a town where until then something like that wasn't even imaginable. Then obviously everybody looks up at that group of people who opened fire on a much stronger enemy, and what do I know? And then of course, stories begin to be told, and that's how it was. I believe the attitude of people was very positive, very favourable, even more than that, people called asking for rifles, for weapons, especially since these lads in HOS were not afraid, they did not fear this much stronger enemy, and they were quite ingenious too. I can tell you, for instance, one incident which added to the HOS reputation. Mostar was a city which was rife with fear, with gunfire and all that. And one day when shells never stopped hitting the town all day, on that building where HOS was and then Vinko or somebody else, I don't know, thought of something, I don't know who exactly, but at any rate, from that area here, one could hear loud, very loud music, that is some songs, which were aimed against the Serbian aggression. As a matter of fact, they put up two or three powerful amplifiers or a thousand volts or something and it helped people, because people were afraid they were in shelters or something, some makeshift shelters and that boosted the morale very much because all of a sudden one could hear music all over the town so these young men, they were ingenious, they were brave, they were not afraid, and I believe that they had a very positive, very favourable influence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How do you interpret the fact that it was Vinko himself who became a HOS commander?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, Vinko, in his younger days, liked to chop wood. I'm sorry but -- and when his father would say or rather to him and to me, "Well, we need some wood," then I would do it in a special way, well, do I a little bit today and perhaps I'll do it tomorrow or perhaps I'll do it in the morning, whereas Vinko had a very simple approach. He would just pick up the axe and chop the wood. So Vinko was a very clear, direct, no particular philosophy, I hope you won't get me wrong but what he did, he applied himself to whatever he had to do and so he simply imposed himself on them. Not to mention his appearance. I mean no mention of that. So it wasn't difficult for him to become a commander. I suppose he has it in him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what -- how did this HOS unit end eventually?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Eventually, it met with a rather inglorious end. After -- well, I'd say its end was very poor. And Vinko was fortunate or unfortunate, it is up to the Chamber to decide, Vinko had 60 or maybe 70 soldiers of Islamic faith or Bosniaks in his unit, and the rest, the 30 or so per cent were Serbs or Croats. Was it a coincidence or not, was it deliberate, I really cannot say, but those were men that he palled up with, those were people that he fought the war against the Serbs and after a while it became a problem in the town itself and we discussed it a hundred times, must have. He didn't really want to talk about it but once we read in some newspaper or other that Mr. Alija Izetbegovic had said how HOS units were the elite units of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and people as people folk as folk, suddenly something began to happen and I take the liberty to say that perhaps he will get angry with me, but when he no longer had the control over the situation, that is the Croats began to feel that they were a minority, Muslims started sporting some special arm bands or some special badges, the Serbs were pretty lost, they didn't know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. which way to turn and at the same time the HVO became the proper army, proper military formation, on the left bank, the Mostar Battalion began to take shape at that time which was the forerunner of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, who were saying that HOS were their own. On the other hand, Vinko didn't know whether to turn left or right, and at some point, I think it all culminated when a visit was paid to Vinko. I was present there, that is a representative of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina or rather that Mostar Battalion, that is of the Muslim army at that particular moment, came to request him that the weapons depot literally be sold, not turned over but sold to the BH Army, and there were some rather disagreeable situations at that time, and Vinko simply lined up his troops and said, "Well, each his own rifle, and join whichever army you like." So I think this was a rather inglorious end to that unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what then happened to him, to Vinko, after that? Did he join somebody else?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Vinko seemed pretty resigned, pretty disenchanted, pretty disappointed at that time, until then he used to walk around the streets and people liked to see him because he was a defender, he defended the town, the streets, the small streets, but then there was this -- these problems, he couldn't understand, whether he had this unit or not and I suppose he must have also earned some enemies because he wasn't one to give in easily. He thought that this unit could resist the enemy but he didn't have no troops or anything when it disbanded so he removed his uniform when the war started.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But did he become politically active, did he join a party did he come to hold some political or military post?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what about you at that time?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Are you asking me about the time when the war with the Serbs ended and then this -- the period that ensued? Well, I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did you do?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Mostar was destroyed city, and I'm a -- I've got technical training, so for me and people of my trade, there was more than enough work for us. From an analysis of the destroyed buildings to plans for the reconstruction, plans for the reconstruction of the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, in March, 1992, Bosnia and Herzegovina proclaimed its independence. Do you know what did Vinko Martinovic think about that at the time? How did he see it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I hope my brother won't hold it against me but I think that he didn't take any sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what was or is your personal view?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding what?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Regarding the fact that Bosnia-Herzegovina was proclaiming its independence and becoming an independent state?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
