utterances.text: Favourable. I think the purpose was pursued by all the republics was to split away from Yugoslavia and that it was viewed favourably.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So do you know, at that time I mean, if Vinko Martinovic in any way whatsoever participated or took part in any political activities related to the establishment of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, he did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you personally participate in some political activities related to Herceg-Bosna, that is Croat Community Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Vinko Martinovic voiced any views regarding the establishment of the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what did the establishment of that -- of that community, the Croat Community Herceg-Bosna, mean to you?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, to me it meant the equality before law of all the peoples in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the first, the second and the third, and the protection of these interests.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you -- did you know what were the views of your neighbours who were of other ethnic backgrounds, Muslims in particular?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I think that they varied. I mean I suppose that if somebody thought differently, I'm not sure that he would tell me that. So people that I worked with, people that I socialised with, I do not think that there were any particularly adverse reactions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In April, 1992, the Croat Defence Council was set up, as the supreme executive, administrative and defence authority of Bosnia-Herzegovina. What did it mean to you in Mostar? Did any changes ensue?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you exactly whether that -- whether we started to fight better against the Serbs or something, but the fact that there was an army on the ground who would be fighting in that war against the Yugoslav People's Army and that was the feeling we had, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know what was your brother's opinion about the Croat Community of Herceg-Bosna -- of the Croats Defence counsel? Did he join the Croat Defence Council? I mean in 1992.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. Vinko was with HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what about you? Did you join the Croat Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did, and I've already said I was with the 4th Battalion of the Croat Defence Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have or did you have any knowledge as to the views of your Muslim neighbours? Did they join the Croat Defence Council?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I was issued with a uniform and boots, and whatnot by a Muslim but one could join only the Croat Defence Council or HOS, so whether a soldier gladly goes to war, I don't know, but whoever joined could join only the HVO at that particular time.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: In April 1993, the first conflicts between Muslims, Bosniaks, and Croats started outside Mostar. Did it find any reflection from what you know on the relations between Croats and Muslims, Bosniaks, in Mostar itself?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, an ordinary man is usually the last to find something out, something that he should perhaps know a little earlier and the same would apply to those events. In Mostar, we didn't have an adequate media coverage, we didn't have enough electricity or water let alone good information, so that this information mostly reached the town as some information that is one would discuss it always with a question mark, whether is it true or not? Did somebody fall out or not? So in Mostar, it did not necessarily mean that it was a war straight away. That is in Mostar it was not really properly covered, not as somebody who would have a distance might do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But from what you know, at that period of time, then, that is after April 1993, was there any harassment of Muslims, their dismissal from work, attacks on their houses in Mostar, especially people of prominence, public figures, do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Listen, if you're asking me about that period when things happened, as they happened in Central Bosnia or whatever went on there, at that time, I think I can say under full responsibility that it was not happening in Mostar. I do not think that anything like that was recorded in Mostar at that time. Now, whether there was something verbal, I cannot know that, but that the house was in flames in Mostar at the same time or a few days after it burnt, I don't know, what did you say, in Ahmici or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I can positively say that that was not the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: From your contacts with your brother, what was his reaction to the news about fighting between Muslims and Croats? I mean in Bosnia, did it affect his attitude towards Muslims in any way?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I'd like to begin by saying I mean when you say "news," well, it wasn't a particularly bombastic news. It again sounded, you know, you talk with people and somebody says, well, you know this nonsense happened everybody's got some weapon, something will happen, some stupid thing will happen, so we didn't really take it that way, that it could escalate and reach Mostar. So how Vinko reacted? Well, at that time, Vinko was involved in his own business, a little bit, and as I have said he was pretty disenchanted and he still behaved like somebody who was been disappointed.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, do you remember the 9th of May, 1993? And if you do, why do you remember it?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course. Yes, I do remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us briefly what did you do that day? What did you go through that day?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: That day, early in the morning, I was on my way back to Mostar, because I'd been to see my parents and my family, and they were in Omis as emigrants. I was to enter that town across a crest, a hill crest called Zovnica, from which you can see Mostar as if in the palm of your hand and I had a friend with me who had also gone to see his family in Makarska and we met on the way. I cannot give you the exact time but I'd say that it could not be after half past 9.00 in the morning, and the first thing was that we were stopped by the military police at Zovnica. They asked me where we were going, who we were, what we were, and we said that we were going home, a little bit taken aback but then we heard that there was gunfire in the town and that it was in disarray, that there was some commotion. So we both reached a neighbourhood restaurant, and in that restaurant, we found already a few dozen people, some in civilian, some in uniforms, a few policemen, some with, some without weapons, and there we learned that there was fire in the -- in the town or more specifically at Rondo, that there was an exchange of fire, that a policeman had already got killed there, that nobody could get to him and, I don't know. So of course, it became unsafe there because there were all sorts of vehicles dashing to and fro, ambulances, private people with rifles and civilians in uniforms running up and down, information, disinformation, noise, and at some point, perhaps after 15 minutes or an hour, you just don't know, time flying by and you really lose a proper sense of it, Vinko turned up with three friends of his. So what's going on, so is it true, is it true that the Muslims have crossed or rather come to Rondo, that there was gunfire all around? And so on. Then a couple of windows on a building right next to the place where we were began to ring and shattered and then we, all of us, well, I can't say like some army but we started moving. And now I have to say this now aloud, we started moving towards the enemy. I want to point out that it was very chaotic, that one didn't know who was firing at whom, who was firing from where, in which building there were troops, that is armed men, in which there were none, and I want to point out that concretely with Vinko were two friends of his I do not know, they were Muslims, who were as lost, as confused, and I suppose much more embarrassed than I was because it was quite clear that they would be firing at Muslims. I want to say that I was with a group of seven, eight men. We were all in civilian clothes, and at some point I found myself next to civilian facilities, that is private houses. And it was the first time in my life that I saw a warrior, a combatant, with a green bandana, who, seeing me, opened fire from his automatic rifle, crying out, shouting, "Allah-u-ekber" and at that place there are still marks on the wall. It was patched up but one can see it easily. And we were there until 4 or 5 clock in the afternoon because we dared not go forward, we dared not go backward. We didn't know what to do. And throughout, whilst all this was going on, this gunfire and all that, and you can hear the ambulances and you can hear cries for help, and the tires screeching and screams round buildings, general din, shouts, snipers, not snipers [as interpreted] and so on and so forth. Around 6.00 in the afternoon that same day, we were near a building which we called the health centre.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Sorry, may I interrupt you for a moment and then we shall move on? Do you remember, Mr. Martinovic, the names of those two men who were with Vinko that day when you saw him and when you -- who you told us were Muslims? Do you remember their names?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. One of them I know just first name and the last name, and the other one I know just the pseudonym or nickname.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to the private session, Your Honour so we can actually hear those names?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said that you moved towards the medical centre. What happened next?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I can only try and continue along the same lines in a nutshell, it was a pitifully sight, you cannot go forward, you cannot go backward. You do not cope. The night is falling, there is shooting all over. In a nutshell it was really chaotic. Later on we met with some other people. And then it was either us or them who came out of certain facilities, and then around 6.00 in the afternoon, I'm not really sure of the time, Vinko came out of somewhere and, with his commanding voice, he said, "This is not the place either for you or for them." And told us to go, to leave. But it was easier said than done. I couldn't go anywhere. I didn't know whether I could go back or whether I could go forward. I didn't know where I would be safe. There was shooting from all the buildings. Somehow, I returned to the same restaurant where I started from. That was our local pub where we used to drink coffee every day. This is where I returned. We continued talking. The night fell but we didn't have any accurate information.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: According to what you saw, the group of people that you were moving with, was that a unit, a formation? Did it have its commander? Did it look like an organised group of people?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I owe you an explanation before I answer this, because some things will obviously not be clear. I was a member of the HOS, like so many others, and I was never stationed in any barracks because there were no barracks, and all of us who had arms carried the arms with us, and we would take our weapons home. When I went home to take my weapon, because there was shooting all over the place, and I believe that it was a logical move, anybody else would have done that, then my neighbour left my building to go -- together with me. He asked me, "What's going on?" I told I don't know. But there seems to be some fighting with the Muslims. That all happened some 250 to 400 metres as the crow flies from the building where I lived. And that was when I saw that fighter, a member of the BH Army, when what happened happened. There was some five or six men, together with me, of whom one of them is today a director of a bank, another one is a -- the owner of a car garage, the third one is the owner of a drive cleaning shop, and I can give you their names if I need to do that. So these were the people who just happened to be there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where exactly did you see the BH Army soldier, on the western bank?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: In the courtyard of a house some 50 metres below the round about, below the Rondo on the western side of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What happened to Vinko on the following days after the 9th of May, 1993? What did he do? Where was he?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Vinko was on the front line. He remained at the place from which he chased me away. He was there with a group of soldiers who reported to him. These were all the men that he was together within the HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: What did you do on the days following the 9th of May?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: To be honest, I was on the street all day long. I hung around the restaurant, because I wanted to obtain as much information as possible. I would rarely see anybody these days, just the people who would go to the place of conflict and then when they would return I would ask them to tell me what they saw.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: So what you saw on the street and based on that, what was the situation in the Western Mostar? What was the security situation? Did the number of troops go up? Did the number of armed men increase?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: In those days, and I would say it was for a month or so, Mostar was transformed and changed. During the war with the Serbs, Mostar was a peaceful town, because it was under a lot of shelling, there was not a lot of moving going on, and you knew which places were more or less safe, and this is where people gathered. There was no -- not much moving but during this subsequent conflict, and for the next month or so, Mostar looked like, I don't know how to describe it, there was a lot of troops, a lot of vehicles, a lot of confused people. There was chaos. The situation was chaos, there was no electricity, there was no water. It is very difficult to describe the situation. However it was a very bad experience and I would not wish that experience upon anybody. We had been through a war already, and the -- this new situation is an experience that nobody wanted to be -- have to go through.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you notice that there was a change of attitude towards Muslims? Were any measures taken against the Muslims who resided in the area under the control of the Croatian Defence Council, during the early days?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The answer is no. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the Muslims in Mostar reacted to the conflict that started on the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I know, of course I know, just like the Croats on the other side, the reaction was fear on both sides, and the most often heard comment would be, "It's nothing. It is much ado about nothing. It will amount to nothing." Because it was so strange that these two people would be waging a war against each other. The most common reaction was this is just stupid. It is just the politicians who did not reach agreement but when they will it will not amount to anything because at the time there was still a lot of Muslims in the HVO they had still not left the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, when are we planning our next break, just to help me to plan for my examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, we could stop here or we could continue to sit for another ten minutes. It depends on how far you're going in your examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Both solutions I find both solutions convenient. So maybe we can take a break now and then I will continue after the break. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We will take a short break. We will take about 20 minutes break. We'll resume at ten minutes to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Mr. Martinovic, this indictment claims that there were 2 persecutions of people from Mostar. The first one after the 9th of May, 1993, and the second one in the early days of July of 1993. Would you agree with these allegations?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Are you referring to the first one or the second persecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let's first talk about the first persecution after the 9th of May, 1993.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: So in May, 1993, I already said that the situation in the town was more than chaotic, so nothing can be excluded. I can't say that something did happen and something did not happen. However, people were running away on both sides. So everybody who had something upstairs and who found himself in the area where the fighting was going on, would run away, on both sides. I personally would have run away. So much about that in the month of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And in July 1993? Or after, rather? After the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Several months into that conflict, when it could already be said that it was actually a war and not a skirmish, that we all hoped for, I believe that on both sides, it was clear that it was not just any conflict but something that would take a long time, and I think at that time it was logical that every member of every side would take to their own respective side. I know for a fact that dozens of Muslims who had realised that it was their place to be with their people, their own way, the same was true of the Croats. I have members of my family whom I painstakingly moved from the left bank to the western side. I believe that the people spontaneously decided it take to their own respective side. I believe that it was not orchestrated it was just a spontaneous reaction. Whether this is persecution, it is very hard for me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Where were you personally at the time, after the 30th of June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: In Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if there were, within the HVO, some instructions about the need to ethnically cleanse the western part of Mostar?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I don't know that, but to be honest, I was not in the position to be given such an instruction or such an order so that I would be aware of such an instruction.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Let's go back to the events that took place on the 9th of May, 1993, and after that day. Can you please tell us whether Vinko Martinovic in any way participated in the persecution of Muslims in Mostar after the 9th of May, 1993?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: According to your knowledge, was it at that time that the Mrmak unit, later on the Vinko Skrobo unit, was established?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to make a mistake in my answer. I don't know what you mean when you say "at that time." But I know for a fact that it was not immediately after the 9th of May, because if it had -- if that had happened during the first days after the 9th of May, then I would have been a member of that unit, so it didn't happen for a month or even longer than that, because during those first early days, it was very hard to know who was doing what. So I -- I -- my answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know how the unit was established?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: On the separation line, i.e. at the place of the conflict, Vinko remained there and people started rallying around him. These people were those same people who had been with him in the HOS, who had remained in Mostar. A lot of them had left Mostar before that. And that, with time, that group of people became a unit. I asked Vinko at some point how come the unit was called Mrmak. Vinko had a dog, a boxer, whose name was Mrmak. I don't think that Vinko really believed in those early days that that unit would stay on, that it would continue. So I think that at the time, it was just a joke for him, in a way. He really did not believe that this unit would be transformed into anything big.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know how did it come about that Vinko Martinovic became the commander of that unit?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I do not know that, but I can make an educated guess. I suppose he was simply got stuck on that separation line, pigheaded as he was, he wouldn't step back, and as people came along, as I have said, he's a natural leader. I suppose he was born that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Were you a member of that unit, ever?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How is it, then, that you know so much about the circumstances, about the situation, in the unit and certain things that happened there on the front line and at their base?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: This last word you used, "base," it was less than 70 or 80 metres from the building that I lived in. I believe that is your answer. I saw my brother regularly. I saw those men. I was simply there. I was present there like many others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge whether some members of that unit, Vinko's unit, participated perhaps in the persecution of Muslims on the 9th of May or later? Do you have any personal knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: On the 9th of May, nobody could expel anyone because on the 9th of May, everybody was firing at everybody else so that on the 9th of May, it never crossed anybody's mind to do anything like it. On the 9th of May, there was nothing like that happened. I can claim that under full responsibility. But after that, a soldier who finishes his shift, leaves the rifle, goes home.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know whether Vinko Martinovic knew about that and what was his reaction to it, if you know that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President I think I've been silent completely up to now but this now goes to the point of pure speculation, his state of mind. I know hearsay is widely accepted by the Tribunal but nonetheless, there are limits.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Seric. You may put your question another way or you may skip this question completely.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will skip that question, Your Honour. No problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did Vinko Martinovic at that time, according to what you know, have any military authority that would allow him to take any decisions concerning the treatment of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: The indictment alleges that the second wave of persecutions happened in July, that is after the 30th of June, in July, 1993. Do you remember what was the situation in Mostar like at that time and what happened to Muslims then?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I believe I've also answered it sometime ago, to that question, at least in part. Muslims wanted to cross to the other bank because the war was going on and the Croats from the east bank wanted to cross to the left bank. The war was going on. And both sides of Mostar, if I may put it that way, were full. If I may put it that way, there was a surplus of people. Muslims must have had 15 or 20.000 refugees from East Herzegovina, Central Bosnia, what Serbs had expelled a few months earlier. The Croats on the right bank must have had 4.000 or 5.000, I didn't count them to give you the exact figure, I do not know but there must have been no less than 4.000 or 5.000 Croats expelled from East Herzegovina, Jablanica, Konjic, east part of Mostar, complete chaos. So I'm not justifying it for one second but everybody, of course, cares about his own roof. I am not justifying it, I'm merely stating facts. So everybody was expelling everybody and forcing everybody out and forcing everybody in.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: And what was Vinko's position at the time? Where was he?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Well, where he always was, at the front line.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: During that period of time, and I'm referring to the period after the 30th of June, 1993, or if you like, at some other period of time during that conflict, did Vinko's attitude towards Muslims change?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely not. Listen, somebody who is born in Mostar, grew up in Mostar, was schooled in Mostar, is the same thing. I mean it's like that even today. You're attitude does not change. So I claim that Vinko's attitude did not change. He still had other Muslims in his unit, just as he had many Serbs during the war against the Serbs. Vinko is simply a child of Mostar, and things like that do not change like that. It is another matter when circumstances are different, when you're at the front line and you have an enemy facing you, then you're not interested in that. But in a normal situation, in normal social relations, then Vinko, and this is not pathetic, Vinko was simply not able to change his idea of somebody overnight or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Then how do you explain the fact that this indictment alleges, and that is what literally the indictment literally stays, Stela and his men, Stelici, pursued the policy of persecution against the Bosnian Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: You asked me that in a relatively short sentence. The important thing to say, before I say anything else, is perhaps that for the duration of the war, the war against the Serbs and the war between the Muslims and the Croats, to put it that way, Vinko never stopped being a warrior, without any political support, without any pedigree and at the same time, without mercy, he was fortunate in the beginning and then unfortunate later on, to have after the -- to have come out of the war against the Serbs and later on against the Muslims, he and his units, as a hero. He was one of the first to pick up his rifle. He fought and all that. And then he ended up as he did. In the second part, Vinko took up the rifle again. So you have a tragic-comic situation I might even say. Up this front line of 30 or 50 metres that is one street, one Bulevar and those boys called to one another across the street, they communicated because they knew one another. They were together either in HOS or the HVO, they were all together so they would shout to one another, "Come on, don't fire," or"throw that tin," or something, and that worked. So very many people because of that wanted to cross from the left to the right and from the right to the left side. It is hard to believe but very many people wanted to take across a bag with food, which is just human. That is somebody whose family is left on the other side, then he says, "Come on, let me through because I've got those my folk. So let me go through." So Vinko could do that. He could stop the fire. He could say his name and say, "Come, don't shoot, because we've got this bloke here who wants to take some food over." So I mean, I know what it sounds like when you say front line, but, no, not really, because this conflict, it was everybody's conflict except those soldiers' conflict, those who fired shots there, and that conduct of Vinko on the line and that's in that second part, I presume drove crazy those who wanted to fight. I'm telling you that. I'm putting it to you. Since at this part of the front line, at this part of the long line because it was common knowledge that one could get through and there would be no fire for five or seven days, it was possible because they would talk together and would agree we won't open fire. Then on the other side, Muslims, would bring units which were not local, which were not from Mostar then they brought from that bank, units made from people, I don't know, from Jablanica or made of those refugees and then regularly in a -- there would be a shell hitting parts of Vinko's units or a bomb or something. Because that is what they suited them, because war agreed with them. And that is why I think that it was at about that time that this play, I won't call it a conspiracy but this play began, this game against Vinko because Vinko saw this war in his own way. He had to be there and he knew what mother, father, children were, and he stood there.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of how there were people who falsely introduced themselves like Stela's men? Stela's boys, Stelici?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: On various occasions, therefore, on various occasions when I personally saw that, and I can give you an example because it's very simple, an example when a few friends approached me and then I spoke to -- with Vinko in order to clear the matter up. So it happened on several occasions. But here I'll give you my personal example. I was in the apartment when one could hear the siren, when one could hear a vehicle, two shots in the air, and there were some Muslims there, and I came out on to the balcony and I have to tell you that I was living on the first floor of that building, there was a very high -- high ground floor and then the first floor which was about the level of a normal second floor. And downstairs there were two guys and I can really say they were lads because neither was over 20, and they had weapons in their hands. And I asked them, "Yes, boys, what do you want?" Are there any Muslims here? Yes, there are. You'll show us who they are. We need to empty. Why do you have to do that? Don't ask. Stela said so. I did not know them. I more or less knew all the Stela's soldiers because when I leave my apartment I have to pass by the base. And again, while perhaps these are some new soldiers, perhaps these are new men. So I tell them, "Lads, nothing doing. And you can tell him that." And I made a sign as if I'd pay or something so to stop playing, or I said, "I'll come downstairs and we shall clear it up." Of course they did not wait for me. I want to point out that in the building in which I lived, and there are 12 apartments, in three of them there were Croat families, the rest were Muslim families. One night, I can mention the last name of the family, I don't think there is anything -- one night, the Badzak family were not in their apartment in the morning. That is, somebody had come and taken them away. And I saw it as my personal defeat, my personal defeat. Afterwards, I spoke over the telephone with Mrs. Badzak and she was nice to me, thanked me for being in the building all the time, because it had yielded some result against the break-ins of those night hordes. She also sent greetings to Vinko and when I asked her if she knew who had taken her away, she said that they were Stelici, Stela's boys. And then I asked her how did she know that, know that they had said that they were his boys, but that she knew that they couldn't be. A third example. My personal friend and friend from work, after the war, against the Serbs, left Mostar and went with his wife to Germany. He's a Croat by ethnicity, and his wife is of Islamic faith. And one day, he called me to ask me, because we were close friends, to ask me to ask my brother to have his soldiers out of his flat and his mother-in-law's flat, because she had been expelled from the -- from the apartment, and driven across the river to the other side, to the east side of Mostar. So I went to Vinko, to tell him that it was no good, that this kind of rumour could be interpreted in different ways, and if something like that happened, it would only confirm the rumour. So if there was such -- because a friend had just called me and he knew that it was his soldiers who were in his mother-in-law's apartment. I personally went to that flat with three of Vinko's soldiers, and in that apartment, we found two soldiers, one was a Croat from Konjic, another was a Croat from Opuzen whom nobody had ever seen before. So I called back Zeljko Juric, my friend from Germany and asked him to tell his mother-in-law to call the international police, which was already in Mostar or some such organisation, and tell them that neither Stela or Stelici were in her apartment, and that in point of fact, she could return to her apartment whenever she liked. Of course, accompanied by that police. And he was quite embarrassed. He apologised. But that was the information that he had received. And later on, I tried to find out more, and I came to know that lady quite well, and she exactly recounted to me the incident which took place in that building, the building that she lived in. And it was like this, roughly: There was a noise on the staircase, on the -- and some questions which were asked, "Stela, shall we try this door, shall we try that door, Stela, Stela?" Somebody making believe that they were asking that. Of course those two soldiers left that flat. Nobody ever punished them for that. That lady returned. She only thanked me, and the whole neighbourhood around her continued to believe that it was Stela who had evicted her from her apartment, and I can give you more examples if you want me to.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But why did they say that they were acting on Stela's behalf rather than some other name?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Again, I think that calls for pure speculation. How Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. does he know why -- unless he had a conversation with the men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, can you rephrase your question?

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, but I withdraw that question. I'll move on, and I think it will be faster.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did Vinko Martinovic do something in that regard? Did he take some steps?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Listen, the last example I gave you shows more or less how it -- what were the measures taken when the culprit would be found. So those two guys who were in the flat simply left and nothing. As for Vinko, on several occasions, he sent some lads in his unit packing. He reported possible excesses. It is a fact, but I personally think that nobody can produce a document that any member of his unit evicted somebody and entered that flat. So if you mean sanctions in that regard, I do not think that so. I do not think there was anyone to apply any measures against.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: But did he perhaps try to communicate with the public by a media?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: When this practice gained momentum, that is whenever something happened in the town people would start shouting that it was done by his unit, by men from his unit, but simply nobody ever brought anyone from his unit to say and take a photograph of him or bring him to court or catch him red-handed. And Vinko and I discussed it a great deal at that time. Vinko is too simple a person to see anything behind that, but I can say freely that we even argued a little bit because I was telling him to give up everything or to find some way to put an end to it. I can freely say that I even forced him, that I drove him crazy with my insistence. So that when he sat down and thought about it, and realised that it was going too far, and then there was an incident at the separation line, then he went to radio Mostar and I believe it was the only broadcast electronic media that had some coverage. And then he said something that is that every crime had a full name, that it shouldn't be associated with his unit, that he was inviting citizens to report it to him, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you have any personal knowledge whether soldiers in Stela's unit ever truly participated in the persecution as is alleged by the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No, I do not have any such personal knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: How did Vinko treat Muslims at that time? And what was your Muslim neighbours' attitude to him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I do not know how it will sound to this Court but Vinko is to this day the favourite of the neighbours, a pet of the neighbours there, both Muslim and Croat. And I believe I've answered your question. I think their attitude is more than favourable.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did your Muslim neighbours turn to him for protection?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. On several occasions, and I have personal knowledge of that, because on several occasions, I went to see Vinko on somebody's behalf, when somebody was threatened, and yes, the answer is on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know or can you give us any specific examples, if you do, can you give us the names, if you want to give us the names we will go to the private session.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we go to private session, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know what happened with Muslims, members of Vinko's unit, the Vinko Skrobo unit?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: One has to admit that there were also Croats who were members of the BH Army, and again, one has to be honest and admit that their parents were not very happy about that fact. The same was true of Vinko's unit, but the only difference being that in Vinko's units, there were a lot of Muslims. After a certain time, in agreement with Vinko, they just crossed the separation line and abandoned the unit for a simple reason. Their families were on the other side. So it didn't make sense for somebody to shoot at the side where his family was, and there were never any problems with that, to do something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did Vinko maintain contact with these men, regardless of the fact that they went to the other side? Did he maintain contacts with them? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I am trying to remember some examples to illustrate my answer. A relative of mine, whose name I can mention, this gentleman died two years ago, but his two children and wife still live, his last name was Sopta and his first name was Tomo, he remained on the left side. He came in touch with me via my friend, a lawyer from the left bank, I can tell his name but not in an open session. And what he wanted to do, he wanted to get away from the left bank, and then I asked Vinko what could be done about that? And Vinko said, "You will wait a few days, and when the troops are changed over, on the other side, then I saw how this was arranged. There was some shouting, there was some arrangements, agreements, there were contacts obviously because these people knew each other.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Throughout all this time, the relevant time, where were you, what did you do, what was your attitude towards Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Where I was, and where I worked, there were also Muslims working with me. So the attitude was always the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if detainees from the Heliodrom were brought to the Vinko Skrobo unit?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know how they came, how they were brought to the unit?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I had an opportunity on one occasion to see a lorry in which they were brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you have the -- a way to find out what the treatment of these detainees was?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: On several occasions, I would go either into town or to work. I would see among those detainees somebody I knew well or some of my acquaintances. A number of times, I would take that person home to have a bath. They were neither hungry nor thirsty. Sometimes they just wanted a cigarette. But all of them wanted a bath. So I would take a number of them to my home to have a bath. And nobody had anything against that. They would be strolling around in the street and if anybody of them could go to it my place to take a bath, then I assumed that everything else was okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you know what they did? What was their task?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: In the part where I saw them, they -- their task would be to clean somebody's courtyard, to clean the vehicles, to repair a bonnet of a vehicle. They would be leaning against a wall. They would be spoke smoking. That is as much as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: You said in that part. Is that close to the medical centre or close to the base?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: The medical centre is the place that I did not visit, for two reasons. My brother wouldn't let me. And the second, I did not have any business being there. So it was close to the base, close to my apartment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you personally know whether, during such work, some of the detainees were either injured or killed?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. I think that nobody did. There were several detainees who were always there, and they would talk to me, and I believe they would have told me if something like that had happened. These are the guys that I would regularly take home to have a bath.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of somebody called Nenad Harmandic and did you know him personally?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: I heard of him. I didn't know him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When did you hear that name?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: When I read the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you then find out who the man was?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No. What I read in the indictment is what I read in the indictment. Then I made some inquiries and it was only then that I found out who he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the destiny of Nenad Harmandic? Do you know personally anything?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you ever talk to your brother about him?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: When was that and where, can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: When I first read the indictment against Vinko, it was published somewhere, I don't know in which paper it was, but all the papers carried that indictment because that indictment was somebody's victory. So everybody read it, not just me. And most people did not understand that indictment, but all of us noticed the name of Harmandic because that was the only name in the indictment. At the time, Vinko was already in prison in Zagreb, and I think that it was the first and last time when I talked to Vinko about that, because before that, and after that, I didn't have the chance to talk to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what Vinko told you about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott?

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm going to object. I know that we have a liberal policy towards hearsay here but at least where I come from, purely self-serving hearsay is highly objectionable. Let me just make the point further this way: This brother could have had an extensive discussion with his brother after the indictment on all sorts of topics and I don't think it would be appropriate for him to come in here and then relate to us secondhand all of his brother's positions on all the allegations against him. I object.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour -- Your Honours, if I may?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, after consultations, we believe that this part of the evidence is not relevant at all and is highly self-serving in this aspect. So we would like to ask to you skip this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise, Your Honour. I don't want to discuss things with you because one does not discuss things with a Trial Chamber, but I really did not understand. What I understood was that I should skip this question. But what preceded that I did not understand. This is a witness. This is not just a brother. This is a witness under an oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We understand that. In some jurisdictions, we have -- there are very strict limits to the testimony of a close relative to the accused. But here, it seems to me we have a very broad discretion to hear this witness. But when we evaluate the evidence given by this witness, we will take that factor into consideration.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I must repeat that I do not understand because it seems that this witness should not have been here in the first place because if he is the accused's -- the brother of the accused, then it goes without saying that he is lying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Seric, as a matter of fact, whatever your client said to his brother has very little weight for the evidence purposes. So if you insist, we could allow you to ask this question to this witness but, as a matter of fact, we put very little weight on this part of the evidence. You have to understand that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I shall skip the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Did you talk to anybody else about that? And what did you learn?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: About what now? I'm confused.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: About the destiny of Nenad Harmandic.

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: During the war in Mostar, there were some very ugly scenes of killings, murders and accidents. I don't know how this is going to sound to you. After a certain while, investigations were started or rumours started circulating. Not knowing who Nenad Harmandic was, in a crowd of people after having read the indictment, friends asked me, "What is it with your brother? What does this it mean is he going to be okay? Is he not going to be okay?" Then somebody said to me, "Hold on. I saw Nenad on so and so date." And the other one says, "Well, I heard that he left here or there." So there were several versions of this event. What my brother told me is not even important.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, can we move to private session for one question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes, we will go to the private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Do you know if Vinko Martinovic took any disciplinary measures against those soldiers who violated the discipline of the unit?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: Any examples?

utterances.speaker: JADRANKO MARTINOVIC
utterances.text: It depends. For example, a soldier would -- who would have been thrown out of the unit would come to me and would tell me, "Can you please talk to your brother? I didn't do anything bad." Then I would know that it was a matter of classical disobedience, which was a classical sin amongst the soldiers. If Vinko was the one who told me that he had thrown somebody out of the unit, then I would know that that soldier had done something major. So when something like that had happened, there was no use of him to report that soldier to either the military or the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. SERIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to move on to another subject but I can see it is 7.00, but I promise to finish tomorrow within the time frame that I said I would, and that is three hours for the direct examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Well, Witness, I'm afraid you have to stay in The Hague for another day, and tomorrow we will continue your testimony. So as I did to other witnesses, during your stay in The Hague, do not talk to anybody about your testimony today, and do not let anybody talk to you about it. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LIU
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume tomorrow afternoon. Yes, Mr. Par?

utterances.speaker: MR. PAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you will allow me just a technical matter regarding this witness, for tomorrow, if I can inform the Trial Chamber, I'm going to mention some numbers. We have submitted, as the Defence to this Trial Chamber, and to the Prosecution, the list of our following witnesses, who belong to the first group, consisting of six witnesses, and we intend to adhere to that sequence in that list we mention that a witness under number 2, who should come second in a closed session. We mentioned that the witness would arrive only tomorrow, and therefore, he can give his testimony -- he may give his testimony the day after tomorrow. What I would like to it announce now is that if Mr. Martinovic's testimony is over tomorrow before the end of the day, then it will not be witness number 2 on the list who will appear tomorrow but witness number 3.
